IN THIS CASE STUDY

01 / THE QUESTION

The business context.

How can a business turn shopping transactions into useful decisions about its customers? The goal was to connect the data pipeline to clear business questions, then communicate the answers through a Power BI dashboard and executive presentation.

02 / EXPLORE THE WORK

ORIGINAL POWER BI REPORT

Original Power BI report. Enlarge the image to inspect the details.

03 / THE APPROACH

From question to evidence.

01

Prepare

Used pandas to explore records, standardize fields, and fill 37 missing review ratings with product-category medians.

02

Structure

Created age groups and purchase-frequency features, and checked redundant promotional fields.

03

Analyze

Loaded prepared data into PostgreSQL and used SQL to investigate customer segments, subscription patterns, and purchasing behavior.

04

Communicate

Built a Power BI dashboard and an executive presentation, linking descriptive findings to actions worth testing.

04 / WHAT I LEARNED

The useful part of the analysis.

01

A subscription opportunity

73% of records are non-subscribed. This suggests an opportunity to test a stronger subscription proposition, rather than assume subscriptions already drive spending.

02

Similar purchase amounts

$59.49 for subscribers versus $59.87 for non-subscribers. The observed difference does not establish a causal effect.

03

Define the segment carefully

3,116 records were classified as loyal under the project’s purchase-history rules. This is a segmentation output, not a measured retention rate.

Test subscription value and targeted merchandising. Evaluate discount effectiveness alongside margins, not sales volume alone.

05 / SCOPE & LIMITATIONS

What the evidence does—and doesn’t—say.

This is a descriptive analysis of the supplied dataset. It does not establish causation, customer retention over time, or the profitability of discounts.
